newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Mexican rebel says peace further away than ever.
newsitem.headline: Mexican rebel says peace further away than ever.

text.p: Peace between leftist Zapatista guerrillas and the Mexican government is further away than ever, guerrilla leader Subcommander Marcos said in an interview published in an Argentine magazine on Saturday.
Marcos told Noticias in an interview conducted in the Mexican jungles in January that the guerrillas were prepared to meet any new government offensive with greater violence than in the past.

Noticias said that the tape of the interview was seized by Mexican government authorities and only returned partially damaged 70 days later on the condition that the journalist leave the country immediately.

"Peace seems further away than ever," Marcos said. "When you have two adversaries locked in war, even though they say they are talking and negotiating, the reality is that they are trying to annihilate each other."

Marcos blamed the Mexican government for the failure of peace talks to end the three-year old uprising in the impoverished southern jungle state of Chiapas. Accusing the authorities of plotting a new military offensive, he warned the guerrillas would fight back.

"If they attacked us again, as they did in 1995, we would have to revise our response. On that occasion we decided to retreat and hide out in the mountains. Now that we're already in the mountains, we would have no other option than to resist and fight," he said.
The Zapatistas will not lay down their arms until their demands for improved conditions for the local Maya indians are met, Marcos said.
"The Zapatista army cannot disappear because that would mean handing over the indigenous villages to the military and the armed groups that are waging a new dirty war," he said.
He said Mexican forces were being advised by Chilean and Argentine experts in intelligence and interrogation, including mercenaries from the United States.
Marcos called on Mexican and foreign civilians to pressure for an end to the conflict.

"Civilian society is more sensitive to the problems of the indigenous community, it tends to oppose the military solution and the use of force by either the government or the EZLN," Marcos said. "We would be closer to peace if that third force pressured the two sides."
Marcos is well-known for his literary musings on the Internet and his hooded features now rival that of legendary Argentine guerrilla Ernesto "Che" Guevara as a Latin American pop art icon.

Asked during the interview if he had listened to a recent compact disc of his speeches set to rap music, he said: "I have been very busy with questions of peace and war. For the moment I am neglecting my artistic career."
The compact disc called "Chiapas" sold out in Mexican cities in March.
